design_detail: NIOSH case series: a journal article summarizing two Health Hazard Evaluations (HHE 1 and HHE 2) of incidents in two US states in 2017 and 2018 in which five police officers became ill during or soon after responses involving illicit drugs. Retrospective: site visits at each agency with interviews of the officers who had symptoms and of others (number not given), held weeks to months after the incidents; review of medical records, agency documentation of the incidents and the forensic laboratory's results for evidence samples; body-camera footage in HHE 2 only (PDF pp. 1–3, 8). Nothing was sampled in the air, on surfaces or on skin; the only biological tests were those the emergency departments chose to do (none for the officer in HHE 1; urine drug screens for the four officers in HHE 2 and blood tests for three of them). One figure (a photograph of materials found in HHE 1), Table 1 (each officer's activities, symptoms, onset and the emergency physician's clinical impression) and Table 2 (substances identified by the forensic laboratory, with weights). No statistics. The article does not say which incident happened in which year or state; its references 10 and 11 are the two evaluation reports, a New Hampshire report on one officer (NIOSH HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and a Virginia report on officers (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018), so HHE 1, with one officer, is probably the New Hampshire incident (editors' inference from the report titles; PDF p. 11). Neither incident is the one in NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (card sc_niosh_2018: two officers, powder from a locked metal box blown into their faces, no opioid identified), which has another number, differs in every detail and is not cited in this article.
can_establish: What happened to five officers in two incidents, as reconstructed from records, interviews and, in one incident, body-camera footage: the circumstances, the symptoms and when they began, the clinical findings and the emergency physicians' impressions, the limited testing of the officers, and the drugs the forensic laboratory identified in evidence from each scene; and the NIOSH authors' interpretation and their views on prevention.
cannot_establish: Whether any officer took in any drug, by which route or in what amount, or what caused the symptoms (opioids, stimulants, other substances, anxiety or perceived risk, or another condition): nothing was measured on the officers or around them, no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl or synthetic cathinones, one officer had no test at all, and perceived risk was not assessed; nor how often responders who meet drugs become ill, since two referred incidents were chosen to illustrate scenarios.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: two incidents for which law enforcement agencies requested NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations of officers' health effects after unintentional exposure to drugs (PDF pp. 2–3), chosen by the authors to illustrate different scenarios that might lead to exposure and health effects (PDF p. 5). The five officers who had symptoms were interviewed, as were others (PDF p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable. How many NIOSH evaluations the two incidents were chosen from is not stated; other evaluations are only pointed to on a NIOSH web page (PDF p. 5).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex, years of service or medical history for any officer. As context only, the introduction cites an estimated 701,000 sworn full-time officers in about 15,300 US agencies in 2016 (PDF p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: Incidents reached NIOSH because officers became ill and their agency asked for an evaluation, and the authors then chose two to illustrate scenarios; incidents without symptoms, or not referred, are not represented. Nothing follows about how often responders who meet drugs become ill, or about how many incidents would show a confirmed exposure if tested.

exposure.measurement: Not measured. HHE 1 (PDF p. 3): during a traffic stop and vehicle search, a gust of wind blew powder from an unlabelled rubber container, opened outside the vehicle, onto the officer, who said the powder was all over the officer and the uniform; the officer wore a short-sleeved uniform and no gloves, brushed the powder off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; emergency medical service (EMS) staff later washed the exposed skin with water. HHE 2 (PDF p. 4): three officers entered a hotel room where drug paraphernalia and powders lay in plain view and the toilet had been heard flushing many times; they wore short sleeves, two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after, and they took turns to fetch and put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen; one of them later worked at headquarters on a computer and with a camera used in the room, and a fourth officer, who never entered the room, handled that camera and other items from the room, which had no visible contamination, and cleaned gear and a vehicle (Table 1, PDF p. 15). All four were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing) before going to hospital. No air, surface, skin or blood sampling.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Unknown amounts of material of unknown concentration. The authors consider breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing, absorption through the skin, or a combination, all possible in both incidents (PDF p. 6). HHE 1 was outdoors in hot, windy weather; HHE 2 was indoors, beside a bathroom where repeated flushing may have contaminated surfaces (PDF p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Forensic laboratory results for evidence from the scenes (Table 2, PDF p. 16), with weights but no concentrations or purities: HHE 1, fentanyl (compressed tan powder, 9.98 g), fentanyl with methamphetamine (tan powder and chunks, 1.56 g: the rubber container the officer opened), methamphetamine (crystals, 0.006 g) and buprenorphine (sealed packages labelled as a sublingual film; one package tested); HHE 2, dibutylone (residue), N-ethylpentylone (powder, solid material and residue, 2.87 g), heroin (powder, 0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl (residue), cocaine and methamphetamine (residue, and liquid in a syringe) and fentanyl (powder and residue, 0.14 g). The Results call the HHE 2 findings opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones (PDF p. 5). The authors note that not every substance at a scene may be sent to the laboratory (PDF p. 6).

comparison.controls: None. The authors set the officers' findings against the textbook signs of severe opioid toxicity (profound lethargy or other depression of the central nervous system; shallow, slow or absent breathing; constricted pupils; slow heart rate; low body temperature) and of stimulant toxicity (PDF p. 5). Others present (the second officer in HHE 1; the two people detained in HHE 2) are not compared.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical histories, anxiety and perceived risk are not reported; the authors say perceived risk was not assessed (PDF p. 6) and that medical conditions not evaluated in the emergency department could not be assessed afterwards (PDF p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Symptoms as the officers reported them; EMS and emergency department records (vital signs, pupils, mental status, electrocardiograms; blood tests for three officers in HHE 2; urine drug screens for the four officers in HHE 2); the emergency physicians' clinical impressions (Table 1, PDF p. 15); the forensic laboratory's identification of evidence samples (Table 2, PDF p. 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: For the HHE 1 officer, vital signs are set against normal values stated in the text (blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg or above defined as abnormal; resting breathing rate 12 to 15 a minute; heart rate under 100; pupils 2 to 4 mm depending on light; PDF p. 3). The urine screens used standard cut-offs (amphetamines 500 ng/mL, cocaine 150 ng/mL); the opiate screen does not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, and most amphetamine screens do not readily detect synthetic cathinones (PDF p. 7). There is no exposure biomarker.
outcomes.operationalization: Health effects are the symptoms that kept the officers from their duties; opioid toxicity is judged clinically against the signs of severe toxicity; exposure is inferred from the circumstances and from what the laboratory identified at the scene, not measured.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The investigators and the clinicians knew the circumstances; the emergency physicians' impressions name possible fentanyl exposure for three officers and possible accidental overdose for one (Table 1).

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics: a narrative account of five officers in two incidents. The numbers reported are the HHE 1 officer's vital signs and timings (PDF p. 3), one HHE 2 officer's emergency department breathing rate of 9 to 20 a minute (PDF p. 4), the onset times in Table 1 (PDF p. 15), the urine screen cut-offs (PDF p. 7) and the evidence weights in Table 2 (PDF p. 16).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Health Hazard Evaluations are done at an employer's request; no protocol is mentioned. Ethics review was judged unnecessary because the evaluations were considered a public health activity; written consent was obtained for the release of medical records (PDF p. 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Vital signs are given as values for the HHE 1 officer but mostly as categories for the HHE 2 officers; when the urine samples were taken, relative to the incident, is not given; which incident happened in which year and state is not stated; the forensic laboratory's methods and detection limits are not given; and the number of NIOSH evaluations from which the two incidents were chosen is not stated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Five officers in two incidents reported non-specific symptoms (disorientation, lightheadedness or dizziness, blurry vision, weakness, warmth, sweating, numbness of both hands and the tongue, headache, feeling drunk, high, groggy or sleepy), beginning within 5 minutes in HHE 1 and about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began in HHE 2; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave one dose of intranasal naloxone. No officer was reported to have depressed breathing; in the emergency department all were alert, none had documented constricted pupils and the electrocardiograms were normal; blood pressure and heart rate were normal to raised, and one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute. No officer had a test able to detect fentanyl: the HHE 1 officer had no laboratory test, and the urine screens of the four HHE 2 officers, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative for every drug class screened. The laboratory identified fentanyl, with methamphetamine, in the powder left in the container that blew onto the HHE 1 officer, and fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in evidence from the hotel room.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors' main conclusion is hedged: the effects were not consistent with severe, life-threatening opioid toxicity, the risks cannot yet be characterized with certainty, and timely prospective toxicological evaluation of affected responders is needed (PDF pp. 1–2, 5, 10). In places the article goes further than its data: the abstract describes the officers as exposed to opioid and stimulant drugs (PDF p. 1), which nothing measured on the officers shows; the Discussion takes one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids were a substantial component of the mixed exposure (PDF p. 5), from one uncontrolled observation in an officer who had no blood test and whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; it lists nausea among the symptoms the officers reported (PDF p. 5), though nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms (PDF pp. 3–4; Table 1, PDF p. 15); and the prevention section says the potential for risk is clear from these investigations and warns against treating the effects as merely a reflection of perceived risk (PDF p. 8), although perceived risk was not assessed (PDF p. 6).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, cited here (reference 30, given as published in Clinical Toxicology) with two other sources for the statement that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible contamination is promptly removed (PDF pp. 6, 12).

The two NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation reports summarized here: New Hampshire (HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and Virginia (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018), both by Chiu, Hornsby-Myers and Trout (references 10 and 11, PDF p. 11); not read.

NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (November 2018), by Jackson, Chiu and Hornsby-Myers: a different incident (two officers, powder from a locked metal box blown into their faces, no opioid identified in the seized items); not cited in this article, whose web references were accessed in October 2018.

Herman et al. cite this article (their reference 9) as a rare case report in which clinical manifestations were not consistent with opioids and none of the officers tested was positive for opioid metabolites (Herman et al., p. 112). The article reports two incidents with five officers; it judges the effects not consistent with severe opioid toxicity while suggesting milder opioid effects and a substantial opioid part for one officer; and its urine screens, negative for opiates, could not detect fentanyl, while one officer had no test (PDF pp. 3–5, 7).

replication.where_it_stands: Two more incidents investigated by NIOSH, written up by authors who also wrote the NIOSH report on file (sc_niosh_2018), in which officers had non-specific symptoms, no objective signs of severe opioid toxicity were recorded, and exposure was never measured; in neither incident was poisoning confirmed or excluded by a test able to detect fentanyl. The authors call for timely prospective toxicological evaluation of affected responders (PDF pp. 2, 9–10); no such study is on file.

funding.funder: None: the authors report no funding source for the work or the preparation of the article (PDF p. 10). The evaluations were done by NIOSH under its Health Hazard Evaluation program (PDF pp. 2, 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (PDF p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are at NIOSH (PDF p. 1), which also issues the fentanyl guidance for emergency responders that the article supports (reference 14, PDF p. 11). Two authors (Chiu, Hornsby-Myers) are also authors of the NIOSH report on file (niosh_2018), so the two sources are not independent. A disclaimer says the findings are the authors' own and do not necessarily represent the views of NIOSH, CDC or the US Department of Health and Human Services (PDF p. 1). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective, protocol-driven investigation of responders who report symptoms after a suspected exposure: blood and urine taken within minutes to hours and analysed by mass spectrometry for fentanyl, its analogues, stimulants and synthetic cathinones; the material contacted collected and quantified, with air, surface and skin-wipe samples; objective signs (breathing rate, oxygen saturation, pupil size, level of consciousness) recorded at first contact; perceived risk and anxiety measured with validated tools; and responders at the same scenes without symptoms as a comparison.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Two incidents referred by agencies and chosen by the authors; there is no sampling frame.
The incidents were chosen to illustrate scenarios, from an unstated number of NIOSH evaluations that were themselves requested because officers fell ill (PDF p. 5).
Five officers; no frequency is estimated.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Circumstances, protective equipment, symptoms and timing are described, but not the officers' ages, sexes or medical histories, the year and state of each incident, or most vital-sign values in HHE 2.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All five officers with symptoms are described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Exposure was not measured; the tests done could not detect fentanyl or synthetic cathinones, one officer had no test, and opioid toxicity was judged clinically.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: Emergency department records exist for all five, but testing differed by officer (none; urine only; blood and urine), interviews took place weeks to months later, and body-camera footage existed for one incident only.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: The five officers with symptoms were interviewed; how many others were interviewed, or declined, is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case reports and small case series without a comparison; most items do not apply to two incidents. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any conclusion about cause, because no exposure was measured, no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl, and the incidents were chosen to illustrate scenarios. The article may be cited, attributed to its NIOSH authors, for: the incidents as reconstructed; the clinical findings recorded, which showed no objective signs of severe opioid toxicity; the absence of any test able to detect fentanyl in the officers; the forensic laboratory's identifications at the scenes; and the authors' statements, including that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible contamination is promptly removed. It may not be cited as a case of confirmed opioid poisoning, as evidence of absorption through the skin, as evidence that the symptoms came from anxiety (not assessed), or for how often such incidents happen.

key_findings.finding: Two NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations, requested by law enforcement agencies, of incidents in two states in 2017 and 2018: NIOSH staff visited each agency, interviewed the officers who had health effects and others, and reviewed medical records, the agencies' documentation of the incident and forensic laboratory results for evidence samples; body-camera footage was available and reviewed only in HHE 2. The interviews took place weeks to months after the incidents.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2, continued on p. 3) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Investigation Limitations, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The two incidents were chosen to illustrate different types of scenarios that might lead to exposure and health effects; other NIOSH evaluations of responders' exposures are pointed to on a web page. The article's references for the two evaluations are a New Hampshire report on one officer (HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and a Virginia report on officers (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 5); references 10 and 11 (PDF p. 11)
key_findings.note: Which incident happened in which year and state is not stated; the report titles suggest that HHE 1 (one officer) is the New Hampshire evaluation. Neither is NIOSH HHE Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (card sc_niosh_2018), which this article does not cite.

key_findings.finding: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, an officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported that it was all over the officer and the uniform; the officer tried to brush it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer reported intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake.

The HHE 1 officer reached the emergency department about 42 minutes after onset, reported mild blurry vision that resolved after several hours, was alert and had no constricted pupils; during transport and the visit the heart rate was 80–85 a minute, the breathing rate 15–21 a minute and the blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104 mmHg; no laboratory tests were done; the symptoms resolved, and the discharge assessment was chemical exposure. The forensic laboratory identified fentanyl and methamphetamine in the powder left in the container (1.56 g) and fentanyl in a compressed tan powder (9.98 g); the Figure 1 legend says material in a paper wrapper beside the container contained fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 1, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 3, continued on p. 4); Figure 1 legend (PDF p. 14); Table 2 and its footnotes (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: HHE 2: four officers became ill during a response to a 911 call about an unconscious person with a possible overdose in a hotel room. Three entered, saw drug paraphernalia and powders scattered in plain view and heard the toilet flushed many times; the person was intoxicated but conscious and refused care. They wore short sleeves; two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after; they took turns to put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen. One went back to headquarters to process a search warrant, using a computer and a camera used in the room; a fourth officer, who did not enter the room, helped there, handling the camera and other items from the room that had no visible contamination.

At headquarters both officers became lightheaded and dizzy; one also felt groggy, with numbness of both hands and the tongue, and the other weak, with headache, blurry vision, sweating, warmth and feeling drunk. The two who stayed at the scene developed symptoms there or soon after leaving; one, with blurry vision, warmth, weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness and feeling drunk, was helped out of the room, slumped against the wall and then to the ground, and was given one dose of intranasal naloxone by a colleague, with rapid improvement. Table 1 gives the onset as about 75 minutes after the initial response and about 3 minutes after helping a detained person (the officer given naloxone), about 25 minutes (at headquarters), about 90 minutes (in the ambulance) and about 30–45 minutes after first handling the equipment (the officer who never entered the room); the emergency physicians' impressions were acute dizziness with possible accidental overdose for the officer given naloxone, and dizziness with possible fentanyl exposure for the other three.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 1 (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Before transport all four HHE 2 officers were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing). None was reported to have depressed breathing. In the emergency department all had normal temperatures and normal to raised blood pressure and heart rate; three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth (the officer who never entered the room) a breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; all were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms showed no abnormality. Three had blood tests that ruled out conditions including volume depletion and low blood sugar; the officer given naloxone had no blood test. The urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates. All four were discharged after several hours of observation, with their symptoms improved.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4, continued on p. 5)

key_findings.finding: In evidence from the hotel room the forensic laboratory identified dibutylone (residue), N-ethylpentylone (powder, solid material and residue, 2.87 g), heroin (powder, 0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl (residue; temporarily placed in Schedule I), cocaine and methamphetamine (residue, and liquid in a syringe) and fentanyl (powder and residue, 0.14 g); the Results summarize these as opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 3rd paragraph, last sentence (PDF p. 5); Table 2 (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge that the officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature. They write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit that continuum, and that the improvement of the officer given naloxone suggests opioids were a substantial component of the mixed exposure; low-level exposure to opioids combined with other drugs, particularly stimulants, might be consistent with the variety of effects, and adulterants or contaminants in illicit drugs might also lead to a variety of effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Health Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms in the Results or Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Perceived risk can be associated with anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure; the relationships between perceived risk, the exposures and the officers' clinical status were not assessed, and the authors suggest adapting validated tools in future investigations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Health Effects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing and absorption through the skin, alone or together, are named as the possible routes, and all were possible in both incidents. The authors state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder, or powder of an analogue, is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (citing three sources, among them the ACMT and AACT statement); that contaminated gloves or hands followed by touching the face can lead to mucous membrane exposure; and that alcohol-based hand sanitizer, as the HHE 1 officer used, may increase absorption of fentanyl powder and should be avoided.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Risk Characterization — Hazard and Exposure, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The negative urine screens do not rule out exposure: routine opiate screens detect opioids derived from the poppy or metabolized to morphine, such as heroin, and will not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl; synthetic cathinones are not readily detected by most amphetamine screens; the amphetamine and cocaine screens of the HHE 2 officers were negative at cut-offs of 500 ng/mL and 150 ng/mL, results below a cut-off being reported as negative; and the timing of testing relative to exposure adds uncertainty.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Risk Characterization — Hazard and Exposure, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: retrospective evaluations, with interviews weeks to months after the incidents; no standardized clinical or toxicological guideline for the clinicians; only the acute emergency department records were reviewed, so other medical conditions could not be assessed afterwards; and toxicological data were not always available because testing followed clinical need. The authors also call these evaluations, to their knowledge, the only organized review of such exposures among emergency responders to date.

Conclusions and prevention: multiple drugs, including opioids such as fentanyl and stimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine, were present at each incident; the effects were not consistent with severe, life-threatening opioid toxicity but needed medical attention and kept the officers from their duties; the authors write that the potential for risk is clear from these investigations, that assuming both that the effects merely reflect perceived risk and that no protective measures are needed endangers responders and the people they help, and that prevention (controls, protective equipment, training on actual against perceived risk) should start now; they call for surveillance, laboratory simulations, guidelines for medical evaluation and timely prospective toxicological testing, noting that serum fentanyl peaks within minutes of an intravenous or transmucosal dose and that urine detection windows vary.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF pp. 1–2); Prevention for First Responders, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 8–9); Next Steps, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 9–10); Conclusion (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: No funding source for the work or the article; the authors declare no conflicts of interest; ethics review was judged unnecessary (a public health activity), with written consent for the release of medical records; all seven authors are at NIOSH.
key_findings.locator: Title block and footnotes (PDF p. 1); Funding (PDF p. 10)

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the officers reported non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness (PDF p. 5), but nausea appears nowhere among the symptoms given for any of the five officers in the Results or Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the symptom list that the authors place on the continuum of opioid effects is not the officers' own; the Results and Table 1 are the ones to cite for the symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: One HHE 2 officer, the one who handled items at headquarters and never entered the room, had an emergency department breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute, whose lower end is below the normal resting range the article gives for the HHE 1 officer (12 to 15 a minute), yet the article states that none of the four was reported to have depressed breathing and does not discuss the low reading or when it was taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: What the reading of 9 reflected cannot be told from the article; the statement that no officer had depressed breathing rests on what was reported, not on this value.

reporting_issues.issue: The years (2017 and 2018) and the states of the two incidents are given only for the pair, never for each incident; only the titles of references 10 and 11 hint at which report belongs to which incident.
reporting_issues.consequence: The date of each incident is unknown; this matters little for the findings but makes it harder to match the incidents with news reports or other evaluations.

reporting_issues.issue: The ACMT and AACT position statement is cited (reference 30) as published in Clinical Toxicology in 2017, volume 56, pages 391–400. Editors' note: the copy on file is the Journal of Medical Toxicology version (13(4):347–351), which Persaud and Jennings (2020) and Herman et al. (2020) also cite; the NIOSH report on file (Jackson et al., 2018, PDF p. 22, printed D-2) cites a Clinical Toxicology version at 56(4):297–300.
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; the PDFs on file point to a second publication in Clinical Toxicology, but at other pages than reference 30 gives, so its pages look like a citation error.

The urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates. All four were discharged after several hours of observation, with their symptoms improved.
